C2.4.note: Strategyproofness is defined by comparing truthful and misreported preferences, so the two are separate objects. The input is nonetheless notated as the preference relation.

C3.1.quote: voters cannot benefit by misrepresenting their preferences
C3.1.note: Strategyproofness is a property of the rule. No analysis models voters actually submitting misreports; manipulation is only used to define the property.

C3.2.note: The paper does not state that voters submit their held preferences in the non-strategic analyses. The intro mentions properties shown 'under the assumption that all voters submit their preferences truthfully' as general motivation only.

C4.1.quote: for every vNM utility function that is ordinally consistent with voter i’s preferences
C4.1.note: Utility is linked to ordinal preferences via consistency, but it is only used to justify stochastic dominance. This is arguably SPEC, but utilities are not used for any voter-welfare notion in the results.

C5.1.quote: requires that f (R, x) = 0 for all preference profiles R and alternatives
C5.1.note: Ex post (Pareto) efficiency and beta-ex post efficiency are efficiency criteria defined and used in the results.

C5.2.quote: An alternative x Pareto-dominates another alternative y in a preference profile R
C5.2.note: Efficiency is evaluated on the preference profile, with no statement relating it to held attitudes.

VOT.quote_behav: voters cannot benefit by misrepresenting their preferences
VOT.note: Strategyproofness quantifies over possible deviations of each voter, so voters are potential manipulators. Information is not specified; dominance-based strategyproofness is independent of it.
